source.title: Primer: Searching for Efficient Transformers for Language Modeling
source.authors: David R. So; Wojciech Ma'nke; Hanxiao Liu; Zi-Hang Dai; Noam Shazeer; Quoc V. Le

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, including appendices. Some figure content is flattened, but the relevant figure results are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures language-model loss against training compute and reports downstream task performance at different compute budgets, using Primer and Transformer variants rather than reproducing the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The study directly reports a power-law relationship between validation loss and compute for optimally sized models, and a fixed-size compute-savings trend. It also reports one-shot task scores at two compute budgets. Other architecture and dataset comparisons are not separate rows unless they measure one of these outcomes. The cited scaling-law results are not recorded as this study's own results.
record.test_reason: Section 4.1 runs its own sweep of 23M–385M models across four architectures. It reports that validation loss at optimal size roughly follows a power law in training compute, corroborating Kaplan et al. (V1). Table 6 gives pretraining perplexity and one-shot scores for 1.9B models at two compute budgets. Across architectures, equal pretraining perplexity goes with near-equal downstream scores (V6). The study is mainly an architecture-search paper, and these are secondary results.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that Primer, mainly through squared ReLU and depthwise convolution in attention, cuts training compute for auto-regressive LMs. Examples are 4.2X vs T5 at 537M and 1/3 compute for matching one-shot performance at 1.9B. They also say its gains follow a power law with quality at optimal sizes, since the loss–compute lines are roughly parallel, and that savings grow with compute at fixed size.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a searched Transformer architecture with Transformer variants and measures validation loss against compute; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that compute savings vary with hardware, library, model family, dataset, training regime, and model size. It also distinguishes fixed-size runs, where savings grow with compute, from optimally sized sweeps, where the architecture lines are roughly parallel.

fits_no_version.finding: Architecture modifications shift the optimal-size loss–compute power-law line up or down while leaving it roughly parallel, i.e. with a similar exponent. Primer's lower line implies a constant compute-reduction factor at optimal sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural changes alter the power-law coefficient but not the exponent of loss vs compute.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed model size, Primer's compute savings over T5 grow with training length (4.2X at 1M steps), because loss curves flatten at fixed size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed model size, architecture compute-savings ratios grow with training compute.

record.problems: The power-law evidence in Figure 7 is presented graphically without numerical fit parameters or uncertainty in the supplied text. The paper notes its models are orders of magnitude smaller than full-scale GPT-3. The one-shot comparison uses averaged scores over 27 tasks, and the study describes that comparison as crude; the MLM comparison is run only once.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A.11 reports scores for 27 individual downstream tasks, but those are not separately listed here; the aggregate QA and multi-choice averages are retained. The associated per-task comparisons and confidence intervals are in Table 6 and Figure 27.

untested.parts: Loss vs parameters or tokens separately. A range of several orders of magnitude (only about 1 order of compute and 23M–385M parameters). No fitted exponent values are reported.
Not tested. No extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
Not tested. Optimal sizes are used but the parameter/token allocation vs compute is not reported.
Not tested. The sweep varies depth, width and FFN ratio, but no effect of shape at fixed parameters is reported.
Not tested. The work is text LM only; the MLM comparison has no scaling curve.
There is no fit of downstream score against loss or scale across many points, and only one model size (1.9B).
Not tested. There is no comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting, schedule or data effects on exponents.

missing.what: Pretraining perplexity at each compute budget (Transformer 15.3 / 14.3, Primer 14.3 / 13.5). This is needed to link the downstream scores to pretraining loss.
Per-task one-shot scores showing non-monotone changes with compute (e.g. ANLI R1, CB, WSC, WiC).

record.verdict_notes: The scaling-law evidence is a small, figure-only replication with no reported exponents, over roughly one order of magnitude of compute, so the V1 support is weak in strength though consistent in direction. R5 is re-linked to none, and the reader's V7 label is dropped, because fixed-size savings ratios are a method comparison, not a test of fit-dependence. The V6 support rests on just two compute points per model.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss against training compute for optimally sized models. It does not separately test loss scaling with parameter count or training tokens while the other quantities are not bottlenecks, nor establish a several-orders-of-magnitude range for the reported power law.
No test of fitting laws on small runs and predicting substantially larger runs.
Does not report a compute-optimal parameter-count/token-count allocation trend or compare how parameters and tokens grow with compute.
Does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to test whether they change loss only slightly.
Experiments concern text language modeling; no tests of other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer power-law forms.

Reports aggregate one-shot task scores at two compute budgets for 1.9B-parameter models, but does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss or scale over a broad range.

Shows that fixed-size compute savings increase with training compute, unlike the constant reduction factor used in the optimal-size derivation. It does not compare fitted exponents across fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, or data setups, or show that published laws disagree.

relationships.condition: Optimally sized decoder-only LMs of 23M–385M parameters, four Transformer variants, about one order of magnitude of TPUv2 compute
relationships.reason: The authors state that loss vs compute at optimal sizes roughly follows l = ac^-k for all four architectures (R1–R4). This is figure-only, with no exponents given.
relationships.display_finding: Loss approximately followed l = ac^−k for all four architectures at optimal sizes.

relationships.condition: 1.9B Transformer+GELU and Primer, aggregate one-shot QA and multi-choice averages at 1/3 vs full pretraining compute
relationships.reason: Aggregate scores rise with compute for both models (R7, R11). The text's Table 6 shows that matched pretraining ppl (14.3) gives near-matched scores across architectures, so downstream tracks pretraining loss.
relationships.display_finding: Both models' aggregate scores improved with compute, and matching pretraining perplexity at 14.3 yielded nearly matched downstream scores across architectures.

relationships.condition: Multi-choice tasks, especially near-chance tasks (ANLI R1–R3, WSC, CB, WiC)
relationships.reason: Multi-choice averages move only about 1.2–1.6 points for 3X compute (R9, R13). Table 6 shows several tasks flat or declining with more compute, e.g. ANLI R1 for Primer 35.5→34.8.
relationships.display_finding: Average scores improve by only about 1.2–1.6 points with threefold compute, while several tasks stagnate or decline, including a Primer ANLI score falling from 35.5 to 34.8.
